title: Unpacking India's Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026: A Blueprint for Growth & Global Investment
content:
# Unpacking India's Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026: A Blueprint for Growth & Global Investment

In today's dynamic global economy, nations are constantly recalibrating their policies to attract capital and foster domestic growth. India, always at the forefront of economic reforms, has introduced a significant legislative change that could reshape its economic landscape. The **Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026**, tabled in the Lok Sabha on August 4, 2026, is a comprehensive piece of legislation aiming to amend the **Income-tax Act, 2025**, the **Finance Act, 2026**, and the **Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**. This isn't just another amendment; it's an omnibus bill, a strategic move designed to boost manufacturing, strengthen digital infrastructure, and provide much-needed tax certainty for global investors.

Let's dive deeper into what this Bill truly proposes and what it means for businesses and the economy. *Kya naya hai isme?*

## Key Reforms: A Deep Dive into the Provisions

The Bill's objectives are clear: mitigate external economic shocks, ensure domestic economic stability, and support key sectors amidst evolving global conditions. The proposed amendments are manifold, touching upon critical areas like electronics manufacturing, digital infrastructure, the diamond industry, business trusts, and even the framework for offshore funds.

### 1. Catalyzing Electronics Manufacturing: Extended Incentives

India's ambition to become a global electronics manufacturing hub gets a significant push. The Bill extends critical tax exemptions that will surely cheer foreign companies.

| Old Provision (Income-tax Act, 2025) | New Provision (Proposed by the Bill) |
| :------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------- |
| Tax exemption for foreign companies supplying capital goods, equipment, or tooling to Indian contract manufacturers of specified electronic goods, with a sunset date of March 31, 2031. | **Exemption extended till March 31, 2041**. The **scope of "specified electronic goods" is widened** to include laptops, tablets, servers, hearables, wearables, and related accessories. |
| No specific exemption for income from storing electronic components in customs-bonded warehouses for supply to Indian contract manufacturers. | **New exemption:** Income from storing electronic components in warehouses in customs-bonded areas, when supplied to Indian contract manufacturers for specified electronic goods, will be exempt for 15 years, until March 31, 2041. |

**Why this matters:** This extension, for almost another decade, provides long-term clarity and encourages foreign companies to set up or expand their contract manufacturing base in India. The expanded definition of electronic goods and the new exemption for warehousing components signify a holistic approach to building a robust electronics supply chain, enabling "just-in-time" delivery and reducing logistical hurdles. It's a clear signal: *aao, India mein banate hain!*

### 2. Simplifying Tax Rules for Data Center Services

The digital economy thrives on robust infrastructure, and data centers are its backbone. The Bill aims to make India an even more attractive destination for global cloud companies.

| Old Provision (Income-tax Act, 2025) | New Provision (Proposed by the Bill) |
| :------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------- |
| Exemption for income of specified foreign companies procuring services from specified data centers, subject to conditions that the foreign company and data center must be notified by the Central Government and the data center must be "owned and operated" by an Indian company. | **Removes notification and approval requirements** for both the foreign company and the data center. **Extends the exemption to data centers that are "leased and operated" by an Indian company**, not just owned. |

**Why this matters:** The previous notification and ownership requirements added layers of bureaucracy. By removing these, the government is streamlining the process, making it significantly easier for foreign cloud providers to leverage India's growing data center capabilities. This move is expected to attract substantial investment into "AI data cities" and expand India's digital footprint.

### 3. Tax Exemptions for the Rough Diamond Trade

India is a global leader in diamond cutting and polishing, and now, the Bill seeks to strengthen its position in the rough diamond trade as well.

*   The Bill proposes to grant **tax exemptions for foreign companies involved in the sale of rough diamonds in notified special zones**. This exemption will apply to foreign companies engaged in diamond mining, sightholders of such companies, and also to brokers, aggregators, or tender and auction entities connected with the sale of rough diamonds. The income arising on or after October 1, 2026, will be eligible for this exemption.

**Why this matters:** This strategic move aims to shift a significant share of the global rough diamond trade to India, fostering a robust financing ecosystem around it. It's about bringing the entire value chain to our shores, creating jobs, and enhancing India's status as a global diamond hub.

### 4. Streamlining Business Trust Dividend Taxation

Business trusts like REITs (Real Estate Investment Trusts) and InvITs (Infrastructure Investment Trusts) are crucial vehicles for infrastructure and real estate investment. The Bill brings much-needed clarity and uniformity here.

| Old Provision (Income-tax Act, 2025 & Finance Act, 2026) | New Provision (Proposed by the Bill) |
| :------------------------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------- |
| Tax exemption on dividends received by unitholders was restricted if the underlying Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) had opted for the concessional tax regime. Surcharge for domestic companies opting for concessional rates was 10%. | **Uniform exemption for unitholders** on dividend income from SPVs, irrespective of whether the SPV has opted for the concessional tax regime. However, a **higher surcharge rate of 25%** will apply to an SPV of a business trust that opts for the concessional tax regime, compared to the 10% for other domestic companies. |

**Why this matters:** This rationalization provides greater tax certainty and predictability for investors in business trusts, which is a big deal for attracting long-term capital into core sectors like infrastructure. While the surcharge for SPVs in the concessional regime is higher, the uniform exemption for unitholders simplifies the overall tax treatment and removes a previous disincentive. *Ab investment mein confusion kum hoga.*

### 5. Rationalizing Safe Harbor for Offshore Funds Managed from India

India's burgeoning fund management ecosystem stands to benefit greatly from the proposed rationalization of safe harbor provisions.

| Old Provision (Income-tax Act, 2025) | New Provision (Proposed by the Bill) |
| :----------------------------------- | :----------------------------------- |
| Eligible investment funds registered outside India but managed from India had to meet numerous conditions (e.g., minimum 25 members, maximum 10% participation interest of a single investor, minimum monthly average corpus of Rs 100 crore, bar on investing more than 25% of the corpus in a single entity) to avoid being treated as having a business connection in India. | **Significantly reduces the number of qualifying conditions** for such funds (from 13 to 5, as per reports). Specifically, conditions like minimum members, maximum single investor participation, minimum monthly average corpus, and restrictions on investment in a single entity have been removed. |

**Why this matters:** This simplification is a massive step towards promoting fund management activity in India. It makes it easier for global investment funds and their managers to operate from India without facing unintended tax exposures. The message is clear: India wants to be a global hub for fund management.

### 6. Amendments to the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007

This amendment, though not directly related to income tax, has significant implications for digital payments in India.

*   The Bill proposes to **amend Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007**, to replace the existing reference to electronic payment modes prescribed under Section 269SU of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Instead, it will refer to "one or more electronic modes of payment as the Central Government may, by notification, specify". Consequently, banks or payment system providers will be permitted to impose charges, such as **Merchant Discount Rate (MDR)**, on such notified electronic modes. This effectively signals the reinstatement of MDR on UPI transactions, with the aim to fund UPI's next phase of growth.

**Why this matters:** This change aims to ensure the sustainability and continued growth of India's robust digital payment infrastructure, particularly UPI. By allowing charges on certain notified electronic payment modes, the government is looking to create a viable revenue model for banks and payment service providers.

### 7. Replacing the Income-tax (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026

It's also important to note that this Bill seeks to **replace the Income-tax (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026**, which was promulgated on June 5, 2026. This Ordinance had already introduced certain tax exemptions, notably for Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) on income from government securities. The Bill now incorporates these measures into the law and validates any actions taken under the Ordinance.

## Concluding Thoughts: India's Vision for a Resilient Economy

The Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, is undoubtedly a forward-looking legislative endeavor. It reflects India's proactive approach to navigating global economic uncertainties and leveraging its strengths to attract high-value foreign investments. From fostering a robust electronics manufacturing ecosystem and boosting digital infrastructure to simplifying compliance for global funds and providing certainty to business trusts, the Bill addresses several crucial pain points.

This is more than just a tax amendment; it's a strategic legislative statement that positions India as a reliable, predictable, and attractive destination for global capital and business. Professionals in finance, law, and manufacturing should pay close attention to the intricacies of this Bill, as its provisions are set to significantly impact their respective sectors. *Aage chal kar, is Bill ka asar poori economy par dikhega.*
